claim: Bedaquiline (BDQ) is an inhibitor of the mycobacterial ATP synthase.
source: Here, we analyzed the effects of bedaquiline (BDQ), an inhibitor of the mycobacterial ATP synthase, on human macrophages.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of BDQ.

claim: BDQ treatment at 5 µg/mL corresponds to the concentration detected in the plasma of TB patients treated with BDQ.
source: We treated human monocyte-derived macrophages from four healthy donors with BDQ at 5 µg/mL, which corresponds to the concentration detected in the plasma of TB patients treated with BDQ (Andries et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Andries et al., 2005.

claim: BDQ at 5 µg/mL did not affect cell viability over an incubation period of 7 days.
source: This concentration did not affect cell viability over an incubation period of 7 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 579 genes were differentially expressed in naive macrophages incubated with BDQ.
source: We found that 579 and 1,495 genes were respectively differentially expressed in naive- and M. tuberculosis-infected macrophages incubated with the drug, with an over-representation of lysosome-associated genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results from the abstract.

claim: 1,495 genes were differentially expressed in M. tuberculosis-infected macrophages incubated with BDQ.
source: We found that 579 and 1,495 genes were respectively differentially expressed in naive- and M. tuberculosis-infected macrophages incubated with the drug, with an over-representation of lysosome-associated genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results from the abstract.

claim: BDQ treatment triggered phagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: BDQ treatment triggered a variety of antimicrobial defense mechanisms, including phagosome-lysosome fusion, and autophagy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an observed effect of BDQ.

claim: BDQ treatment triggered autophagy.
source: BDQ treatment triggered a variety of antimicrobial defense mechanisms, including phagosome-lysosome fusion, and autophagy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an observed effect of BDQ.

claim: BDQ effects were associated with activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB).
source: These effects were associated with activation of transcription factor EB, involved in the transcription of lysosomal genes, resulting in enhanced intracellular killing of different bacterial species that were naturally insensitive to BDQ.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a mechanism underlying BDQ effects.

claim: TFEB is involved in the transcription of lysosomal genes.
source: These effects were associated with activation of transcription factor EB, involved in the transcription of lysosomal genes, resulting in enhanced intracellular killing of different bacterial species that were naturally insensitive to BDQ.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TFEB function.

claim: BDQ enhanced intracellular killing of different bacterial species that were naturally insensitive to BDQ.
source: These effects were associated with activation of transcription factor EB, involved in the transcription of lysosomal genes, resulting in enhanced intracellular killing of different bacterial species that were naturally insensitive to BDQ.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an experimental finding.

claim: BDQ could be used as a host-directed therapy against a wide range of bacterial infections.
source: Thus, BDQ could be used as a host-directed therapy against a wide range of bacterial infections.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: 2–28% of TB patients develop mild liver injury during treatment with first-line drugs.
source: Such side-effects can become critical when antibiotic treatment is long and involves several drugs, as in the treatment of tuberculosis (TB), where 2–28% of patients develop mild liver injury during treatment with first-line drugs (Agal et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Agal et al., 2005.

claim: TB patients are more vulnerable to reactivation and reinfection after treatment completion.
source: For example, after treatment completion, TB patients are more vulnerable to reactivation and reinfection of the disease, suggesting therapy-related immune impairment (Cox et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cox et al., 2008.

claim: INH induces apoptosis of activated CD4+ T cells in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB)-infected mice.
source: INH induces apoptosis of activated CD4+ T cells in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB)-infected mice (Tousif et al., 2014) and leads to a decrease in Th1 cytokine production in household contacts with latent TB under preventive INH therapy (Biraro et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tousif et al., 2014.

claim: INH leads to a decrease in Th1 cytokine production in household contacts with latent TB under preventive INH therapy.
source: INH induces apoptosis of activated CD4+ T cells in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB)-infected mice (Tousif et al., 2014) and leads to a decrease in Th1 cytokine production in household contacts with latent TB under preventive INH therapy (Biraro et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biraro et al., 2015.

claim: RIF has immunomodulatory properties and acts as a mild immunosuppressive agent in psoriasis.
source: RIF has immunomodulatory properties and acts as a mild immunosuppressive agent in psoriasis (Tsankov and Grozdev, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsankov and Grozdev, 2011.

claim: RIF reduces inflammation by inhibiting IκBα degradation and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation.
source: RIF reduces inflammation by inhibiting IκBα degradation, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation (Bi et al., 2011), and Toll-like receptor 4 signaling (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bi et al., 2011.

claim: RIF reduces inflammation by inhibiting Toll-like receptor 4 signaling.
source: RIF reduces inflammation by inhibiting IκBα degradation, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation (Bi et al., 2011), and Toll-like receptor 4 signaling (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: PZA treatment of MTB-infected human monocytes and mice significantly reduces the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
source: PZA treatment of MTB-infected human monocytes and mice significantly reduces the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Manca et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Manca et al., 2013.

claim: Several anti-TB drugs bind to the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and may impact host defense.
source: Recently, Puyskens et al. showed that several anti-TB drugs bind to the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and may impact host defense (Puyskens et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Puyskens et al., 2020.

claim: Macrophages are the primary cell target of MTB.
source: Macrophages are the primary cell target of MTB, which has evolved several strategies to survive and multiply inside the macrophage phagosome, including prevention of phagosome acidification (Sturgill-Koszycki et al., 1994), inhibition of phagolysosomal fusion (Armstrong and Hart, 1975) and phagosomal rupture (Simeone et al., 2012; van der Wel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MTB infection.

claim: MTB prevents phagosome acidification.
source: Macrophages are the primary cell target of MTB, which has evolved several strategies to survive and multiply inside the macrophage phagosome, including prevention of phagosome acidification (Sturgill-Koszycki et al., 1994), inhibition of phagolysosomal fusion (Armstrong and Hart, 1975) and phagosomal rupture (Simeone et al., 2012; van der Wel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sturgill-Koszycki et al., 1994.

claim: MTB inhibits phagolysosomal fusion.
source: Macrophages are the primary cell target of MTB, which has evolved several strategies to survive and multiply inside the macrophage phagosome, including prevention of phagosome acidification (Sturgill-Koszycki et al., 1994), inhibition of phagolysosomal fusion (Armstrong and Hart, 1975) and phagosomal rupture (Simeone et al., 2012; van der Wel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Armstrong and Hart, 1975.

claim: MTB causes phagosomal rupture.
source: Macrophages are the primary cell target of MTB, which has evolved several strategies to survive and multiply inside the macrophage phagosome, including prevention of phagosome acidification (Sturgill-Koszycki et al., 1994), inhibition of phagolysosomal fusion (Armstrong and Hart, 1975) and phagosomal rupture (Simeone et al., 2012; van der Wel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Simeone et al., 2012 and van der Wel et al., 2007.

claim: BDQ is a diarylquinoline that specifically inhibits a subunit of the bacterial adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase, decreasing intracellular ATP levels.
source: BDQ is a diarylquinoline that specifically inhibits a subunit of the bacterial adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase, decreasing intracellular ATP levels (Andries et al., 2005; Koul et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andries et al., 2005 and Koul et al., 2007.

claim: BDQ has 20,000 times less affinity for human ATP synthase than for bacterial ATP synthase.
source: It has 20,000 times less affinity for human ATP synthase (Haagsma et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haagsma et al., 2009.

claim: The most common side effects of BDQ are nausea, joint and chest pain, headache, and arrhythmias.
source: The most common side effects of BDQ are nausea, joint and chest pain, headache, and arrhythmias (Diacon et al., 2012; TMC207-C208 Study Group et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Diacon et al., 2012 and TMC207-C208 Study Group et al., 2014.

claim: 186 genes were upregulated by BDQ in naive macrophages.
source: The expression of 579 genes was affected by BDQ (FDR < 0.05, Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2), with 186 being upregulated and 393 being downregulated.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results.

claim: 393 genes were downregulated by BDQ in naive macrophages.
source: The expression of 579 genes was affected by BDQ (FDR < 0.05, Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2), with 186 being upregulated and 393 being downregulated.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results.

claim: The gene set upregulated by BDQ in naive macrophages was significantly enriched for genes associated with lysosome, phagocytic vesicle membrane, vacuolar lumen, hydrolase activity and lipid homeostasis.
source: The gene set upregulated by BDQ was significantly enriched for genes associated with lysosome, phagocytic vesicle membrane, vacuolar lumen, hydrolase activity and lipid homeostasis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene-set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The BDQ-resistant MTB strain carried an Ala63→Pro mutation in subunit c of the ATP synthase.
source: The selected clone, which carried a Ala63→Pro mutation in subunit c of the ATP synthase (Andries et al., 2005; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), had a similar generation time to wild-type bacteria when cultured in 7H9 liquid medium, although we observed a slower growth after 7 days of treatment.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and cited from Andries et al., 2005.

claim: The BDQ-resistant MTB strain had a similar generation time to wild-type bacteria when cultured in 7H9 liquid medium.
source: The selected clone, which carried a Ala63→Pro mutation in subunit c of the ATP synthase (Andries et al., 2005; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), had a similar generation time to wild-type bacteria when cultured in 7H9 liquid medium, although we observed a slower growth after 7 days of treatment. (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The MIC99 for susceptible MTB was 0.07 µg/mL.
source: As expected, the MIC99 (defined as the concentration required to prevent 99% growth) for susceptible MTB was 0.07 µg/mL, a value similar to previously published study (Andries et al., 2005), while the MIC99 of the BDQr-MTB was 36 µg/mL.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement consistent with published data from Andries et al., 2005.

claim: The MIC99 of the BDQr-MTB was 36 µg/mL.
source: As expected, the MIC99 (defined as the concentration required to prevent 99% growth) for susceptible MTB was 0.07 µg/mL, a value similar to previously published study (Andries et al., 2005), while the MIC99 of the BDQr-MTB was 36 µg/mL.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of the resistant strain.

claim: 499 genes were upregulated by BDQ in MTB-infected macrophages.
source: The expression of 1,495 genes was affected by BDQ (FDR < 0.05, Figure 1A, Figure 1—source datas 3 and 4), with 499 being upregulated and 996 being downregulated.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results.

claim: 996 genes were downregulated by BDQ in MTB-infected macrophages.
source: The expression of 1,495 genes was affected by BDQ (FDR < 0.05, Figure 1A, Figure 1—source datas 3 and 4), with 499 being upregulated and 996 being downregulated.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results.

claim: More genes were affected by BDQ treatment in MTB-infected cells than in naive macrophages.
source: More genes were thus affected by BDQ treatment in MTB-infected cells than in naive macrophages.
evidence: This is a comparison of the RNAseq results between the two conditions.

claim: MTB infection induces an extensive remodeling of the transcriptome.
source: This probably reflects the fact that MTB infection induces an extensive remodeling of the transcriptome (Barreiro et al., 2012; Tailleux et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barreiro et al., 2012 and Tailleux et al., 2008.

claim: 452 genes were differentially expressed in both naive and MTB-infected cells upon BDQ treatment.
source: 452 genes were differentially expressed in both naive and MTB-infected cells upon BDQ treatment with an over-representation of lysosome-associated genes (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—source data 7).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 1C and heatmap in Figure 1D.

claim: BDQ treatment resulted in a 30% decrease in basal glycolysis and glycolytic capacity compared to untreated cells.
source: After incubation with BDQ, we observed a 30% decrease in basal glycolysis and glycolytic capacity compared to untreated cells (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse Extracellular Flux analyzer data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: BDQ treatment increased the levels of phosphatidylinositols.
source: We observed an increase of phosphatidylinositols upon incubation with BDQ (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No significant changes were observed in the levels of phosphatidylethanolamines, phosphatidylglycerols, or cardiolipins upon BDQ treatment.
source: No significant changes were observed in the levels of phosphatidylethanolamines, phosphatidylglycerols, or cardiolipins.
evidence: This is a statement of the lipid profiling results.

claim: 38 lysosome-related genes were differentially expressed by BDQ in naive macrophages.
source: We identified 38 and 54 differentially expressed genes by BDQ, respectively in naïve- and BDQr-MTB infected cells (FDR < 0.05, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 3A.

claim: 54 lysosome-related genes were differentially expressed by BDQ in BDQr-MTB infected cells.
source: We identified 38 and 54 differentially expressed genes by BDQ, respectively in naïve- and BDQr-MTB infected cells (FDR < 0.05, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 3A.

claim: At 18 hr and 48 hr post-BDQ treatment, fluorescence intensity of LysoTracker was substantially increased in macrophages incubated with BDQ compared to DMSO-treated cells (1.7 and 5.4 times more, respectively).
source: However, at 18 hr and 48 hr post-treatment, fluorescence intensity was substantially increased in macrophages incubated with BDQ compared to DMSO-treated cells (1.7 and 5.4 times more, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 18 hr and 48 hr post-treatment, BDQ-treated macrophages showed a dose-dependent increase in fluorescence intensity of DQ-Green BSA (up to 5.5 times more than untreated cells).
source: At 18 hr and 48 hr post-treatment, we observed a dose-dependent increase in fluorescence intensity upon treatment with BDQ (up to 5.5 times more than untreated cells, p<0.01, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The combination of PZA with BDQ was highly bactericidal on MTB, leading to a 83% decrease in colony forming units using 50 µg/mL PZA.
source: We confirmed that the combination of PZA with BDQ was highly bactericidal on MTB, leading to a 83% decrease in colony forming units using 50 µg/mL PZA.
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BDQ alone at 1 µg/mL had no antibacterial activity.
source: This decrease was not a result of an additive effect between the two drugs, as BDQ alone at 1 µg/mL had no antibacterial activity.
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No synergy was found between BDQ and PZA on the BDQ-resistant mutant cultivated in Middlebrook 7H9 liquid medium.
source: We also found no synergy between BDQ and PZA on the BDQ-resistant mutant cultivated in Middlebrook 7H9 liquid medium (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by optical density measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The potentiation of PZA activity by BDQ is most likely due to the effect of BDQ on the host cell, and in particular on the increase of lysosomal acidification.
source: Thus, the potentiation of PZA activity by BDQ is most likely due to the effect of BDQ on the host cell, and in particular on the increase of lysosomal acidification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing synergy in cells but not in liquid culture.

claim: BDQ did not potentiate the activity of ethambutol (EMB), isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin (RIF).
source: We found that BDQ did not potentiate the activity of ethambutol (EMB), isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin (RIF) in either case.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 556 genes were differentially expressed in cells stimulated with heat-killed bacteria and exposed to RIF.
source: 556 and 752 genes were differentially expressed in cells stimulated with heat-killed bacteria and exposed to RIF and PZA, respectively (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source datas 1–5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 752 genes were differentially expressed in cells stimulated with heat-killed bacteria and exposed to PZA.
source: 556 and 752 genes were differentially expressed in cells stimulated with heat-killed bacteria and exposed to RIF and PZA, respectively (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source datas 1–5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the RNAseq results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The lysosomal pathway was not induced upon RIF or PZA treatment.
source: We classified these genes by performing gene-set enrichment analysis and confirmed that the lysosomal pathway was not induced upon RIF or PZA treatment (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene-set enrichment analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Only two genes belonging to the lysosomal pathway were upregulated by RIF.
source: The expression of only two genes belonging to this pathway was upregulated by RIF, and only one by PZA, compared to 46 whose expression was modulated by BDQ (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagrams in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Only one gene belonging to the lysosomal pathway was upregulated by PZA.
source: The expression of only two genes belonging to this pathway was upregulated by RIF, and only one by PZA, compared to 46 whose expression was modulated by BDQ (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagrams in Figure 5B-C.

claim: 46 lysosomal genes were modulated by BDQ.
source: The expression of only two genes belonging to this pathway was upregulated by RIF, and only one by PZA, compared to 46 whose expression was modulated by BDQ (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagrams in Figure 5B-C.

claim: None of the tested antibiotics (AMK, EMB, INH, PZA, RIF) were able to increase LysoTracker staining.
source: Consistent with these results, none of these antibiotics were able to increase LysoTracker staining (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: All three autophagy inhibitors (BAF, CQ, 3-MA) prevented the increase in LysoTracker staining upon BDQ treatment.
source: After 2 days, we analyzed LysoTracker staining as a read-out of lysosome activation using flow cytometry and observed that all three inhibitors prevented the increase in staining upon BDQ treatment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: BDQ treatment resulted in an increase of LC3B puncta per cell at 18 hr and 48 hr post-treatment.
source: We observed an increase of LC3B puncta per cell at 18 hr and 48 hr post-BDQ treatment using confocal microscopy (Figure 6B–C), which was associated with the detection of lipidated LC3 (LC3-II), the form of LC3 recruited to autophagosomal membranes, and with a decrease in sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1) or p62 levels (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: BDQ treatment was associated with the detection of lipidated LC3 (LC3-II).
source: We observed an increase of LC3B puncta per cell at 18 hr and 48 hr post-BDQ treatment using confocal microscopy (Figure 6B–C), which was associated with the detection of lipidated LC3 (LC3-II), the form of LC3 recruited to autophagosomal membranes, and with a decrease in sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1) or p62 levels (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: BDQ treatment was associated with a decrease in p62 levels.
source: We observed an increase of LC3B puncta per cell at 18 hr and 48 hr post-BDQ treatment using confocal microscopy (Figure 6B–C), which was associated with the detection of lipidated LC3 (LC3-II), the form of LC3 recruited to autophagosomal membranes, and with a decrease in sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1) or p62 levels (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: BDQ significantly reduced the number of BDQ-resistant MTB bacteria in infected cells.
source: BDQ significantly reduced the number of bacteria (measured by CFU) in cells infected with BDQ-resistant MTB.
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The effect of BDQ on reducing bacterial numbers was completely inhibited by the autophagy inhibitors 3-MA and BAF.
source: This effect was completely inhibited by the autophagy inhibitors 3-MA and BAF (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: S. aureus and S. Typhimurium are resistant to BDQ, even when exposed to high concentration of the drug (20 µg/mL).
source: We confirmed that these two species are resistant to BDQ, even when exposed to high concentration of the drug (20 µg/mL, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial growth data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When macrophages were incubated with BDQ and then infected with S. aureus and S. Typhimurium for 24 hr, a substantial decrease in bacterial survival rates was observed.
source: However, when macrophages were incubated with BDQ and then infected with S. aureus and S. Typhimurium for 24 hr, we observed a substantial decrease in bacterial survival rates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The autophagy inhibitor 3-MA was unable to revert the macrophage resistance to S. aureus infection upon BDQ treatment.
source: To determine if autophagy is involved in this antibacterial activity, we incubated the infected cells with the autophagy inhibitor, 3-MA, and were unable to revert the macrophage resistance to S. aureus infection upon BDQ treatment (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Upon incubation with BDQ, an increase in the amount of NO2- was detected in the culture supernatant of macrophages.
source: Upon incubation with BDQ, we detected an increase in the amount of NO2-, a stable derivative of NO, in the culture supernatant of macrophages (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by Griess reaction assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: When cells were treated with L-NAME, an inhibitor of nitric oxide (NO) synthesis, S. aureus-infected cells were unable to effectively control infection upon incubation with BDQ.
source: When the cells were treated with N(G)-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME), an inhibitor of nitric oxide (NO) synthesis, S. aureus-infected cells were unable to effectively control infection upon incubation with BDQ (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: hERG RNA was not detected in human monocyte-derived macrophages by RT-qPCR.
source: Therefore, to further understand the molecular mechanisms underpinning macrophage activation by BDQ, we determined if human monocyte-derived macrophages expressed hERG, but were unable to detect hERG RNA by RT-qPCR (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: No changes in mitochondrial membrane potential were observed when macrophages were incubated with BDQ for 6, 24 and 48 hr.
source: No changes were observed when macrophages were incubated with the BDQ for 6, 24 and 48 hr (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by TMRM staining data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No change in basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and non-mitochondrial respiration was detected in cells treated with BDQ for 24 hr and 48 hr as compared to untreated cells.
source: We also measured the oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and detected no change in basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and non-mitochondrial respiration in cells treated with BDQ for 24 hr and 48 hr as compared to untreated cells (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: No difference in mitochondrial superoxide was observed upon BDQ treatment.
source: Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) are involved in the regulation of several physiological and pathological processes, including autophagy (Sena and Chandel, 2012). We thus stained for mitochondrial superoxide using the MitoSOX dye in BDQ-stimulated cells. Again, we saw no difference upon antibiotic treatment (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by MitoSOX staining data shown in Figure 8D and cited from Sena and Chandel, 2012.

claim: Incubation with the antioxidant glutathione (GSH) or with its precursor N-Acetyl cysteine (NAC) did not prevent lysosome activation and the killing of S. aureus by BDQ.
source: Incubation with the antioxidant glutathione (GSH) or with its precursor N-Acetyl cysteine (NAC), which prevent the formation of mitochondrial ROS and reactive nitrogen species (RNS), did not prevent lysosome activation and the killing of S. aureus by BDQ (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: It is unlikely that BDQ alters mitochondrial function in human macrophages.
source: Based on these results, it is unlikely that BDQ alters mitochondrial function in human macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple negative results regarding mitochondrial function.

claim: At 18 hr post-treatment, TFEB was mainly localized in the nucleus of BDQ-treated cells.
source: We therefore analyzed the cellular localization of TFEB, using confocal microscopy. At 18 hr post-treatment, TFEB was mainly localized in the nucleus of BDQ-treated cells (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: An increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration was observed in macrophages treated for 18 hr with BDQ.
source: In agreement with these studies, we observed an increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration in macrophages treated for 18 hr with BDQ (Figure 9C), and confirmed that this intracellular calcium accumulation was required for antibiotic-induced TFEB translocation to the nucleus and lysosomal gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by calcium measurement data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Upon treatment with BAPTA-AM, a cell permeable Ca2+ chelator, TFEB remained localized in the cytoplasm of BDQ-treated cells.
source: Upon treatment with BAPTA-AM, a cell permeable Ca2+ chelator, TFEB remained localized in the cytoplasm of BDQ-treated cells (Figure 9D), and we were unable to detect changes in the expression of a panel of lysosomal genes, previously identified as differentially expressed in macrophages incubated with BDQ (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The increased bactericidal activity against S. aureus was abrogated in the presence of BAPTA-AM.
source: The increased bactericidal activity against S. aureus was also abrogated in the presence of BAPTA-AM (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: In TFEB-silenced cells, BDQ slightly increases the LysoTracker staining.
source: In TFEB-silenced cells, BDQ increases slightly the LysoTracker staining (Figure 9G), and the expression of atp6v0a1, mcoln1, scarb1 or trpm2 (Figure 9H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: TFEB activation is required for better control of S. aureus and MTB upon BDQ treatment.
source: We also infected macrophages with S. aureus and MTB, and showed that that TFEB activation is required for better control of both pathogens upon BDQ treatment (Figure 9I–J).
evidence: This is supported by CFU counting data shown in Figure 9I-J.

claim: BDQ induces the recruitment of TFEB to lysosomal gene promoters.
source: We next evaluated the recruitment of TFEB to the promoters of some lysosomal genes. As expected, BDQ induces the recruitment of TFEB to these promoters (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BDQ reprogramed cells into potent bactericidal phagocytes.
source: Genome-wide gene expression analysis revealed that BDQ reprogramed cells into potent bactericidal phagocytes.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: BDQ is a cationic amphiphilic drug, consisting of a hydrophobic ring structure and a hydrophilic side chain with a charged cationic amine group.
source: BDQ is a cationic amphiphilic drug, consisting of a hydrophobic ring structure and a hydrophilic side chain with a charged cationic amine group (Diacon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of BDQ's chemical structure supported by a citation to Diacon et al., 2012.

claim: Cationic amphiphilic drugs can accumulate in lysosomes through ion trapping.
source: Cationic amphiphilic drugs can accumulate in lysosomes through ion trapping (de Duve et al., 1974).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cationic amphiphilic drugs supported by a citation to de Duve et al., 1974.

claim: Lysosomotropic compounds usually increase the lysosomal pH and thus decrease lysosomal enzyme activity.
source: Such lysosomotropic compounds usually increase the lysosomal pH and thus decrease lysosomal enzyme activity (Kazmi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lysosomotropic compounds supported by a citation to Kazmi et al., 2013.

claim: BDQ triggers lysosomal activation, upregulating the expression of genes coding for hydrolases and for subunits of the lysosomal proton pump v-ATPase.
source: However, our results reveal instead that BDQ triggers lysosomal activation, upregulating the expression of genes coding for hydrolases and for subunits of the lysosomal proton pump v-ATPase.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the RNAseq and functional assays.

claim: Pre-clinical studies have shown that BDQ may induce phospholipidosis.
source: Pre-clinical studies have shown that BDQ may induce phospholipidosis, potentially explaining some of the drug's observed toxicities (Diacon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diacon et al., 2012.

claim: Phospholipidosis is characterized by the accumulation of phospholipids in lysosomes, resulting in impaired lysosome function.
source: Phospholipidosis, which is characterized by the accumulation of phospholipids in lysosomes, resulting in impaired lysosome function, is common upon treatment with cationic amphiphilic compounds (Shayman and Abe, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about phospholipidosis supported by a citation to Shayman and Abe, 2013.

claim: In BDQ-treated macrophages, only an increase in the amount of phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate was observed.
source: In BDQ-treated macrophages, we only observed an increase in the amount of phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate.
evidence: This is a summary of the lipid profiling results.

claim: 28 genes involved in phospholipid metabolism were differentially expressed in BDQ-treated macrophages.
source: In accordance with this idea, 28 genes involved in phospholipid metabolism were differentially expressed in BDQ-treated macrophages.
evidence: This is a statement of the RNAseq results.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol phosphates regulate many cellular functions, including endosomal trafficking, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) export, autophagy, and phagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: Phosphatidylinositol phosphates regulate many cellular functions, including endosomal trafficking, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) export, autophagy, and phagosome-lysosome fusion (De Matteis et al., 2013; Levin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about phosphatidylinositol phosphates supported by citations to De Matteis et al., 2013 and Levin et al., 2017.

claim: mTORC1 binds to and phosphorylates TFEB, resulting in its cytosolic sequestration.
source: mTORC1 binds to and phosphorylates TFEB, resulting in its cytosolic sequestration (Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012; Settembre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TFEB regulation supported by citations to Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012 and Settembre et al., 2012.

claim: Upon starvation or lysosomal stress, mTORC1 is released from the lysosomal membrane and becomes inactive.
source: Upon starvation or lysosomal stress, mTORC1 is released from the lysosomal membrane and becomes inactive (Lamming and Bar-Peled, 2019; Lawrence and Zoncu, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC1 regulation supported by citations to Lamming and Bar-Peled, 2019 and Lawrence and Zoncu, 2019.

claim: The release of lysosomal Ca2+ activates the phosphatase calcineurin, which de-phosphorylates TFEB and promotes its nuclear translocation.
source: The release of lysosomal Ca2+ activates the phosphatase calcineurin, which de-phosphorylates TFEB and promotes its nuclear translocation (Medina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TFEB activation supported by a citation to Medina et al., 2015.

claim: TFEB binds to CLEAR (coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation) elements within the promoters of genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis and activates their expression.
source: TFEB then binds to CLEAR (coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation) elements within the promoters of genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis and activates their expression (Lamming and Bar-Peled, 2019; Lawrence and Zoncu, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TFEB function supported by citations to Lamming and Bar-Peled, 2019 and Lawrence and Zoncu, 2019.

claim: 85 genes containing CLEAR elements were up-regulated 18 hr after incubation with BDQ.
source: We found that TFEB translocates from the cytoplasm to the nucleus in BDQ-treated cells, with the concomitant up-regulation of 85 genes containing CLEAR elements 18 hr after incubation with the drug.
evidence: This is a statement of the RNAseq results.

claim: BDQ accumulated primarily in host cell lipid droplets.

claim: BDQ can accumulate at the lipid membrane of liposomes and act as a H+/K+ ionophore.

claim: BDQ increases the expression of mucolipin 1 gene (mcoln1).

claim: Lysosomal Ca2+ is released through MCOLN1 and activates calcineurin, which binds and dephosphorylates TFEB.

claim: INH and PZA promote autophagy activation and phagosomal maturation in MTB-infected murine macrophages.

claim: Metformin increases the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and stimulates phagosome-lysosome fusion by activating the 5′-adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
source: For example, metformin, an FDA-approved drug for type II diabetes, increases the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and stimulates phagosome-lysosome fusion by activating the 5′-adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Singhal et al., 2014), and recent studies suggest that metformin provides better outcomes in TB patients, especially those with diabetes mellitus (Yew et al., 2019).

claim: Metformin provides better outcomes in TB patients, especially those with diabetes mellitus.
source: For example, metformin, an FDA-approved drug for type II diabetes, increases the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and stimulates phagosome-lysosome fusion by activating the 5′-adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Singhal et al., 2014), and recent studies suggest that metformin provides better outcomes in TB patients, especially those with diabetes mellitus (Yew et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yew et al., 2019.

claim: The product of the enhanced intracellular survival (Eis) gene limits ROS generation.

claim: BDQ can bypass MTB escape mechanisms and allow more effective control of bacterial infection.
source: Our results clearly show that BDQ can bypass these escape mechanisms and allow more effective control of bacterial infection.

claim: BDQ potentiates the activity of other anti-TB drugs, independently of its bactericidal activity on MTB.
